text: Cherry Hospital is an inpatient regional referral psychiatric hospital located in Goldsboro, North Carolina, United States, and operates as one of three psychiatric hospitals under the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services. It serves 38 counties in the eastern region of North Carolina and is part of the Division of State Operated Healthcare Facilities, which manages 14 state-operated healthcare facilities providing care for adults and children with mental illness, developmental disabilities, and substance use disorders. The hospital’s treatment units include Adolescent, Adult Acute Admissions, Geriatric Admissions, Psychiatric Rehabilitation, and Psychiatric Medical, offering care for individuals with complex acute needs not available in their local communities. Originally established in 1877, the facility was created to serve Black mentally ill individuals, with land purchased on April 11, 1878, two miles west of Goldsboro, described by Governor Zebulon Baird Vance as ideal due to its elevation, cultivation, and central location for the Black population. The first patient was admitted on August 1, 1880, under the name "Asylum for Colored Insane," and the institution later changed names to Eastern North Carolina Insane Asylum, Eastern Hospital, and State Hospital at Goldsboro before being renamed Cherry Hospital in 1959 in honor of Governor R. Gregg Cherry, who expanded mental health services and hospital infrastructure during his administration. The original bed capacity was seventy-six, but over one hundred patients were housed by Christmas 1880. On March 5, 1881, the Eastern North Carolina Insane Asylum was incorporated with a board of nine directors, and a separate building for tubercular patients was established; a building for criminally insane individuals opened in 1924. For the first 85 years, Cherry Hospital exclusively served the Black population of North Carolina and remained the only mental hospital for them until the mid-1960s. In 1965, in compliance with the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the hospital began serving all races, with Black patients transferred to regional hospitals and white patients from other regions admitted to Cherry. The hospital’s early treatment was custodial, with able-bodied patients working on the farm; by 1960, Cherry Farm had 2,300 acres of cultivation including fruit trees, an apple orchard, vegetables, and sugar cane, with livestock such as hogs, chickens, turkeys, and cows, supplying 70% of the hospital’s beef and milk, eggs, and pork (except cured bacon), with no products sold except hides. In 1884, a battery was purchased for electricity, and an occupational therapist was hired in 1932, though therapy remained largely farm-based, laundry, kitchen, and yard work. During the 1930s and 1940s, standard medications included laxatives, castor oil, salts, aspirin, and sedatives; hydrotherapy was attempted but abandoned, and seclusion in 6’x9’ steel cages was used until removed in 1956. Chapel services were not available until the early 1950s, with patients allowed to visit churches in Goldsboro under supervision. By 1955, tranquilizing medications revolutionized treatment, leading to increased discharges and shorter hospital stays, while the resident population remained stable at approximately 3,000 between 1950 and 1965, with a peak occupancy of about 3,500. During its first 100 years, the hospital served 91,045 patients. The hospital remained segregated until 1965, when it began serving all races from the 33 counties in the Eastern Region. Two cemeteries are located on the old campus: one behind the Chase Laundry Building (1905–1928) and one behind the McFarland Building (earliest interment 1927); approximately 700 graves are marked with upright brass crosses bearing patient names and dates, and a monument in memoriam was dedicated on June 3, 2004. It is known that over 3,800 people have been buried on the grounds since 1913, with the two cemeteries not accounting for burials between 1880 and 1905. North Carolina was twelfth among the original 13 colonies to pass legislation for a state hospital, influenced by Dorothea Lynde Dix’s advocacy in 1848, which emphasized humane care and cost savings; only two asylums were built before the 20th century: Broughton Hospital and Cherry Hospital. A Founders Gallery exhibit in the New Cherry Hospital honors Dix’s contributions. In fall 2016, the old facility at 201 Stevens Mill Road closed and was replaced by a new Cherry Hospital at 1401 West Ash Street, Goldsboro, approximately one-half mile from the old site, on a 171-acre tract covering 51 acres. The new facility, designed by Perkins+Will and constructed by Archer Western Contractors, LTD, is a single three-story building of about 410,000 square feet (9.4 acres of floor space), including residential patient care units, therapy and medical facilities, and administrative areas. Total funding of $138,325,814 came from special indebtedness bonds approved by the North Carolina General Assembly. A groundbreaking ceremony occurred on October 1, 2010, with Governor Beverly Perdue and Secretary Lanier M. Cansler, and a dedication ceremony on August 30, 2016, attended by Governor Pat McCrory, Secretary Rick Brajer, and Deputy Secretary Dale Armstrong. The old campus consisted of multiple buildings; the new hospital offers expanded services and capacity in one building, including a modern laboratory, dental and radiology departments, internal and external courtyards, a treatment mall (the "Hope and Wellness Center") with magnetically hung flexible pictures, gymnasium, library with computers, cosmetology and barber shops, and anti-ligature doors and tempered glass. Patient transfers began in late September 2016, and a press release on October 5, 2016, confirmed all patients had been safely moved and were residing in the new facility by September 29, 2016. Cherry Hospital serves 38 Eastern North Carolina counties, including Beaufort, Bertie, Bladen, Brunswick, Camden, Carteret, Chowan, Columbus, Craven, Cumberland, Currituck, Dare, Duplin, Edgecombe, Gates, Greene, Hertford, Hyde, Johnston, Jones, Lenoir, Martin, Nash, New Hanover, Northampton, Onslow, Pamlico, Pasquotank, Pender, Perquimans, Pitt, Robeson, Sampson, Scotland, Tyrrell, Washington, Wayne, and Wilson. The hospital employs licensed psychiatrists, internal and family medicine physicians, and mid-level practitioners providing short and long-term mental health care for adolescents, adults, and geriatric patients, with comprehensive treatment involving physical and diagnostic services and therapeutic approaches such as group, behavior, milieu, occupational, recreational, and creative arts therapies. The new facility includes the Riverbend School, an accredited program for adolescents aged 12 to 17, with small-group classrooms for multi-age and grade levels, including regular and special education, and liaison teachers working with parents, guardians, and home-school personnel. Following the move, Cherry Hospital expanded its capacity by more than 100 beds, now operating as a 300-bed facility capable of serving 130+ adults, 28 adolescents, 35 geriatric patients, 10 medical psychiatric patients, and 104 psychiatric rehabilitation patients, with 12 patient care units containing 228 bedrooms (one bathroom per room), 146 private bedrooms, and 82 semi-private bedrooms. The hospital is accredited by the North Carolina Medical Society for Continuing Medical Education (CME) and by the American Nurses Credentialing Center’s Commission on Accreditation (ANCC) for continuing nursing education, and provides continuing education for psychologists, social workers, and teachers through partnerships with Area Health Education Centers (AHEC) Eastern, Southeast, Southern Regional, and North Carolina Psychological Association. Cherry Hospital is affiliated with thirteen nursing schools, offering clinical rotations for students to gain experience in mental health care. It also has affiliations with colleges and universities for internships in social work, psychology, teaching (exceptional children), dental hygiene, pharmacy, therapeutic recreation, and occupational therapy, and serves as a teaching site for psychiatry residents, fellows, and medical students at the Brody School of Medicine at East Carolina University and Campbell University, with clinical faculty appointments. The Cherry Hospital Museum, located at 201 Stevens Mill Road on the old campus, displays documents, photographs, and artifacts detailing the history of the 1880 psychiatric hospital for African American mentally ill individuals from all 100 counties of North Carolina. Due to damage from Hurricane Matthew in October 2016, the museum closed on January 13, 2017, and all artifacts were moved to storage, with plans to rotate them in exhibits at the Founders Gallery in the new hospital and to feature them electronically on message boards throughout the new facility. The Cherry Foundation, a not-for-profit and tax-exempt organization established March 31, 1997, and granted 501(c)(3) federal tax-exempt status, is a separate entity from the hospital and uses tax-deductible contributions directly for patient therapeutic care. The hospital’s geographic coordinates are 35°23′24″N 78°01′44″W.
